newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China quickly stamps power on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China quickly stamps power on Hong Kong.

text.p: China will quickly stamp its rule on Hong Kong with a show of force -- 4,000 People's Liberation Army troops crossing the border on ships, helicopters and armour just hours after the British handover on July 1.
Future leader Tung Chee-hwa's office announced late on the Friday that the troops, spearheaded by armoured cars, would sweep in at dawn, on the tail of night-long handover festivities.
Hong Kong's stock market had just closed at a record high, signalling a wave of public optimism for a prosperous future under Chinese rule.

Governor Chris Patten condemned the move as "a most appalling signal to send to the people of Hong Kong", who are still chilled by images of armoured personnel carriers and green-uniformed troops used in the massacre of unarmed students in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
Britain's Foreign Office said it may send a "negative signal" to the world.

Although Beijing will be responsible for Hong Kong's defence, and there was no doubt it would send a large force, few had expected it to risk inflaming local sensitivies so rapidly with such a blunt military statement.
"We don't seed so many, and we don't need them coming in such a fashion, by air, land and sea," exclaimed grim-faced legislator Emily Lau.
"Come on -- the people of Hong Kong are worried about the PLA."

The troops will enter shortly after the popularly-elected legislature is dissolved, and while U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, British Prime Minister Tony Blair and a host of foreign leaders are still in town.
Chinese naval vessels will churn through waters crossed a few hours earlier by the British royal yacht Britannia carrying Patten and heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles on their way home.
Earlier on Friday, kilted soldiers of the Black Watch bade farewell to 156 years of colonial rule over Hong Kong with a skirl of bagpipes.

But their lament was drowned out by the ring of cash registers as stock investors piled into Beijing-backed "red chip" and other companies and drove the Hang Seng index to an all-time closing record 15,196.79.
The People's Liberation Army already has 196 advance troops in Hong Kong and another 509 will join them shortly before the handover ceremony at midnight (1600 GMT) on June 30.
The number of mainland troops that will pour in on July 1 is larger than any figure given so far.
They will be accompanied by 10 naval ships, six helicopters, 21 armoured cars and 400 other vehicles.
"I do think that it is most unfortunate that this decision has been made. We will continue to make representation and hope that this decision is reversed," Patten said.
"It doesn't sound to me the right sort of signal to send to the international community, and above all I think it is a most appalling signal to send to the people of Hong Kong."
China's Ministry of Defence declined to comment, maintaining its tradition of secrecy.
"We don't know anything about this," said one official of the ministry's foreign affairs bureau.
In Taiwan, the final target of China's reunification effort -- and still unnerved by Chinese military threats during presidential elections last year -- official reaction was muted.
As strings of flags of China and the new Hong Kong -- bearing the emblem of the bauhinia flower -- were strung along main roads, dignitaries began arriving for an extravagant end-of-empire party.
Among them was former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, who signed the 1984 agreement that hands Hong Kong back to China.

Signs of political unease bubbled beneath the surface, focused on the doomed outgoing legislature, to be replaced by a Beijing-picked chamber. Pro-democracy actists such as Lau and Martin Lee will be dumped.
"There is apprehension now as to the possible, and even very likely, loss of some of our freedoms," Lee told Cable News Network (CNN).

Charges of "perfidious Albion" have been flying, with democracy leaders accusing Britain of betrayal over its decision to follow the lead of the United States and send its Hong Kong envoy to the swearing-in of the new legislature.
Journalists expressed fear for the future of press freedom under Chinese rule and said self-censorship was spreading like an insidious disease.
"The signs do not seem positive. We hope we are proved wrong," the Hong Kong Journalists Association said in a report.
